summary: Instagram is carrying the channel: most Hindi videos get 1,200-1,400 views there, while YouTube Shorts mostly gets under 60 views. The best videos are short, surprising 'sensor can't see/hear but still works' explainers about relatable gadgets and hobby robots (gyro robot, clap switch, PIR). Weak ones are generic 'how does X work?' questions on everyday items, such as lift doors, taps, smoke detectors and touchscreens, and these get little reach on either platform.
winningPattern: Hindi Shorts on hands-on maker subjects (robots, clap switch, PIR, mic, IR) with a bold, counterintuitive claim as the hook, such as 'X can't see/hear/think, yet it works' or 'without X the robot falls'. Titles are short and punchy, in Hinglish, with one emoji, and often use a 'Nahi... Sirf...' contrast. Instagram is the main growth platform, and YouTube only picks up the clap switch and PIR videos, which are searchable and curiosity-driven.
doMore: Open with a contradiction or a bold claim ('Nahi... Sirf...') instead of a plain 'Kaise kaam karta hai?' question
Make more robot and Arduino-module videos (gyro, line follower, IR obstacle, clap switch), which get the best likes, saves and shares
Do follow-ups to winners: a clap switch part 3 and PIR or gyro variations, since a sequel to a hit tends to hold its audience
Show a quick physical demo in the first 2 seconds and end with a clear takeaway worth saving or sharing
Test the YouTube titles and thumbnails of the Instagram hits separately, since the same topic gets far fewer views there
stopDoing: Generic everyday-appliance explainers (lift door, washroom tap, smoke detector, mall door) that repeat the same sensor idea
Posting near-duplicate topics (two smoke detector videos, two automatic tap videos, two IR-in-dark videos) within days of each other
Switching to English, since the one English video got only 161 views on YouTube and nothing on Instagram
